text: I have changed my mind about ambition. text: August is the month I trust least. It has the warmth of summer and the face of summer but underneath it is making preparations. text: We should talk about boredom more seriously than we do. Not the boredom of having nothing to do — that's easily solved — but the deeper kind, the kind that persists through activity, that arrives in the middle of parties, that sits at the back of your mind while you're doing exactly what you wanted to do. This boredom is a signal, I think, though I have not yet determined what it signals. Some people treat it as a failure of the self, something to medicate or schedule away. But I've come to believe it might be the psyche's honest report on the distance between your actual life and the one you're obscurely expecting. The tragedy is that we rarely stop long enough to ask what the boredom is pointing at. We reach instead for the phone, for noise, for the next thing. And the thing being pointed at recedes a little further. This seems like an important problem and we mostly treat it as a minor inconvenience.

text: The summer I was eleven we found a dog at the end of our road and kept it for three weeks before its owner came. The dog was old and smelled like creek water and we named it Captain. text: It is possible to miss a place you never lived. text: My position on this is probably unpopular but I'll state it plainly: I do not believe most people who say they love mornings. text: The night before her wedding she can't sleep and goes to sit on the fire escape in her pajamas. The city is doing what the city always does, indifferent to the specificity of her situation. text: What I remember most about learning to drive is not the mechanics of it but the specific fear of my father in the passenger seat. text: There are days when the bureaucracy of being alive feels particularly oppressive. text: My son asked me last spring why we have to die and I said, honestly, that I don't know, and then I said some things about biology and about stars and about how nothing that works the same way forever stays interesting, and he listened politely in the way of a seven-year-old listening to an adult explain something they haven't asked about. text: Friendship in middle age requires making arrangements. There are calendars to be consulted, distances to be driven, babysitters to be secured and dinner reservations and the whole logistical armature of people with too many obligations and not enough margin. I sometimes miss the days when seeing someone meant walking thirty feet down a dormitory hallway. And yet there is something in the arranged friendship, the one that costs something to show up for, that I've come to value in ways I couldn't have when everything was effortless. We chose this, against the friction. The friction is part of the message. I think what we're telling each other, every time we make the arrangements and keep them, is that we still regard each other as necessary. Which, past forty, is not nothing. It might be everything.

text: The Library of Alexandria did not burn in a single catastrophic night. That image, so satisfying in its drama, is a retrospective myth. What actually happened was slower and more dispiriting: decades of neglect, reduced royal funding, the gradual emigration of scholars to Rome and Pergamon, and a series of smaller destructions spread across centuries. Caesar may have accidentally torched a warehouse of books near the harbor during his siege in 48 BCE. Theophilus, the bishop, destroyed the Serapeum in 391 CE. The Arab general Amr ibn al-As may have ordered the remaining collections burned in 642 CE, though this account is contested. What the slow death of Alexandria teaches us is not about the fragility of knowledge, but about the fragility of the institutions that support it. Libraries do not die in fires. They die when the people who funded them stop caring, when the scholars stop coming, when the books stop being copied. The dramatic conflagration is a more comfortable story because it assigns blame to an enemy and a moment. The truth requires us to look at the grinding mundanity of institutional decline.

text: The cave paintings at Lascaux were discovered in September 1940 by four teenagers following a dog into a hole in the Dordogne hillside. They emerged into a chamber whose walls moved with aurochs, horses, deer, and ibex rendered in red ochre and manganese dioxide with a vividness that had waited seventeen thousand years for witnesses. The discovery came in the first autumn of the German occupation of France, and there is something almost unbearable in that coincidence: at precisely the moment Europe was proving what humans are capable of doing to each other, four boys with a lamp were standing in testimony to what humans had once been capable of making. The paintings were opened to the public in 1948, and the crush of tourism quickly introduced carbon dioxide, heat, and green algae that began eating the pigments. The caves were closed in 1963. Now a replica stands nearby, meticulously reproduced, and visitors file through a simulation of the original while the real paintings recover in darkness, tended by climate-control systems, breathing again in the silence they kept for so long.

text: Zoroastrianism shaped the Western imagination in ways its practitioners could never have anticipated. The religion founded by Zarathustra in the steppes of ancient Iran, sometime between 1500 and 600 BCE depending on which scholar you ask, introduced a cosmology built on the struggle between Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord of light and truth, and Angra Mainyu, the destructive spirit. This dualism, with its attending concepts of a final judgment, the resurrection of the dead, and the arrival of a savior figure at history's end, flowed into Judaism during the Babylonian exile, then into Christianity and Islam. The apocalyptic tradition in Western religion is, in no small part, a Persian inheritance. The faith also produced some of history's more striking practical ethics: Zoroastrians were forbidden from defiling the sacred elements of fire, water, and earth, which precluded both cremation and ground burial. The solution was the Tower of Silence, an elevated circular platform where the dead were exposed to vultures. Practicality and theology fused into a practice that struck every outside observer as either profound or appalling, usually both.

text: Brunelleschi solved the dome of Florence's cathedral through a method so radical that when he presented it to the operai, the committee of works, they assumed he had lost his mind. The dome of Santa Maria del Fiore spanned an octagonal opening 143 feet across with no supporting centering, no internal scaffolding, no precedent in the modern world. His solution involved a double-shell structure, a herringbone brick pattern that made each horizontal course self-supporting as it rose, and a series of chains and sandstone rings to contain the outward thrust. He kept the precise details secret throughout construction, fearing that competitors would steal his innovations. He also invented the perspective demonstration and designed his own hoisting machines, which Vasari would later call miraculous. The dome was completed in 1436, four years before Brunelleschi's death, and it remains the largest masonry dome ever built. What makes the achievement strange is not just its engineering but its ambition: the Florentines began their cathedral in 1296 confident that they or their descendants would solve the problem of covering it. They built the hole first and found the answer later. That is either hubris or a remarkable act of collective faith in human ingenuity.

text: The Norse concept of wyrd is routinely translated as fate, but the translation loses something essential. Wyrd, from the Old English verb weorthan, to become, carried a sense of active unfolding rather than passive predestination. It was less a fixed destination than a current, something one moved within rather than toward. The Norns who wove it at the base of Yggdrasil were not recording events that had already been decided but spinning the very substance of what would occur, moment by moment. This is why heroic Norse literature is not fatalistic in any despairing sense. Beowulf knows he will die fighting the dragon. He goes anyway. The going is not futile because wyrd is not about outcomes; it is about the shape of one's becoming. A man who faces his doom with courage has woven himself well, whatever the result. Modern readers often find Norse mythology bleak because of Ragnarok, the twilight of the gods, but the gods fight at Ragnarok knowing they will lose, and their fighting is the point. The world the mythology describes is one in which meaning is generated by confrontation with necessity, not by escape from it.

text: Salt made Venice possible. The lagoon city that would become one of history's great maritime empires began as a collection of fishing communities who had one exportable resource in a world where preserving food meant survival: they could evaporate seawater. By the ninth century, Venice controlled salt distribution across the Adriatic and used that leverage to extract trading privileges from the Byzantine Empire that no other Western city possessed. Salt revenue funded the galleys that protected those trade routes. The trade routes brought spices, silk, and glass-making techniques from the East. The glass went to Murano, where the furnaces were relocated in 1291 to prevent fires, and where Venetian craftsmen developed techniques for producing clear glass that transformed European optics and, by extension, the history of lenses, spectacles, and eventually telescopes. The great paintings of Titian and Bellini were made possible, in a sense, by those tidal flats where Venetian laborers raked salt crystals in the heat. Economic history rarely yields clean chains of causation, but this one holds: the shallow water, the mineral deposit, the preserved fish, the negotiated privilege, the accumulated capital, the cultural efflorescence. One resource, long enough, becomes civilization.

text: The Stoic philosopher Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations with no intention of publishing them. They were private notes, composed in Greek while on campaign along the Danube frontier in the 170s CE, intended as a discipline of self-correction rather than a philosophical treatise. The text circles and returns and contradicts itself because it is a practice, not an argument. Marcus reminds himself, repeatedly, of the same things: that time is short, that fame is empty, that other people's faults should occasion pity rather than anger, that the rational faculty is the only thing truly one's own. The repetition suggests these were not truths he had mastered but truths he was struggling to keep hold of while managing an empire beset by plague and war. The Meditations survived by chance, in a single manuscript tradition, and were first printed in 1559. What makes them strange is the gap between their author's position and their content. Marcus commanded perhaps a million soldiers. He corresponded with kings. And yet the private document he left behind is obsessively concerned with smallness: the smallness of reputation, the smallness of the self, the smallness of everything when measured against time.

text: The Silk Road was never a road. It was a shifting network of routes across Central Asia that changed with political conditions, the rise and fall of oasis cities, and the preferences of individual merchants who rarely if ever traveled the full distance from China to Rome. The term itself was coined by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877, long after the routes had ceased to function as described. What actually moved along these paths was not primarily silk but ideas: Buddhism traveled from India to China along the same corridors that carried glazed ceramics westward. Paper moved west from China and transformed Islamic scholarship before eventually reaching medieval Europe. Plague bacilli moved both directions. The Mongol Empire's pax Mongolica in the thirteenth century created a brief period of safe transit from one end of the continent to the other, which is why Marco Polo's journey became possible when it did. The routes then declined as the Mongol polities fragmented and Ottoman expansion made overland passage difficult, which created the economic pressure that sent Portuguese sailors south around Africa in search of a sea route to the spice trade. The Silk Road's end was, indirectly, what produced the age of European exploration.

text: The development of polyphony in medieval European music was theologically controversial in ways that are hard to reconstruct from inside a culture that takes harmony for granted. Pope John XXII issued a decree in 1324 attacking the new style of composition practiced in the Ars Nova, complaining that composers were cutting the plainchant melodies into short fragments, filling the music with rapid runs, and deploying hockets, the technique of dividing a melody between voices so that one sings while the other breathes, creating a hiccupping texture. The complaint was that this intricacy was distracting worshippers from the sacred text. Underneath the aesthetic argument lay a theological one: the unison of plainchant, a single melodic line sung together, expressed the unity of the congregation. Polyphony, with its crossing voices and competing lines, expressed something else, something more individual, more complex, more of the world. The church lost the argument. By the time of Josquin Desprez in the late fifteenth century, sacred polyphony had become the highest musical form in Western Europe, and the texture of multiple voices weaving together had come to seem not worldly but transcendent, a sonic image of divine order rather than its disruption.

text: Mohenjo-daro was organized with a tidiness that has no parallel in the ancient world. The city of perhaps forty thousand people, flourishing in the Indus Valley around 2500 BCE, had a grid of streets with standardized brick sizes used consistently across hundreds of miles of settlements, a sophisticated drainage system that ran beneath the roads, and public baths whose plumbing rivals anything in Rome, built two thousand years earlier. The uniformity of weights and measures across the Indus Civilization suggests a degree of administrative standardization that would not be seen again in the region until the Maurya Empire. Yet the civilization left almost no evidence of kings, temples, or monumental rulers. There are no pyramids, no royal tombs, no colossal statuary of divine autocrats. The cities seem to have been governed by something, but nothing in the archaeological record clearly shows what. This is among the most tantalizing absences in all of history: a civilization orderly enough to standardize bricks across a subcontinent, but apparently uninterested in the conspicuous display of power that everywhere else accompanied such organization. The script remains undeciphered. The people remain voiceless. The drains work.

text: Caravaggio killed a man in a brawl in Rome in May 1606. The man was Ranuccio Tomassoni, and the circumstances of the fight remain disputed: a gambling debt, an argument over a tennis match, possibly a woman. Caravaggio fled the city under a capital sentence and spent the remaining four years of his life moving through Naples, Malta, and Sicily, producing masterpieces at each stop while running from justice. The paintings he made in exile are among his greatest, and they are haunted by violence and suffering in ways his earlier work, however dramatic, was not. In the Decollation of Saint John the Baptist, painted in Malta in 1608, the executioner has already done his work and is reaching for his knife to finish separating the head, while a servant holds out a platter. It is the largest painting Caravaggio ever made, and in the corner, uniquely in his career, he signed it in the Baptist's blood. Whether this was guilt, bravado, or something stranger is unknowable. He was granted a papal pardon in 1610 and set out for Rome to receive it. He died of fever, or possibly poison, on the journey north, age thirty-eight, before the news reached him.

text: The haiku as a literary form emerged from a longer tradition of collaborative linked verse called renga, in which poets would compose a chain of verses together, each picking up and transforming the images left by the last. The hokku was the opening verse of such a chain, the one that set the season and the mood, and it fell to the most honored poet present to compose it. Matsuo Basho, working in the late seventeenth century, elevated the hokku into an independent form and invested it with a gravity it had not previously possessed. His most famous poem, the one about the old pond and the frog, enacts in seventeen syllables a philosophy about the relationship between stillness and disruption, the eternal and the momentary. The sound of the frog entering the water, the splash, is both an event and the absence of event; it breaks the silence and creates it. Basho traveled constantly, partly out of genuine wanderlust and partly because the form demanded it: haiku required seasonal particularity, the specific quality of light in a specific place at a specific time. You cannot write honestly about autumn in Edo while sitting in spring in Kyoto. The journey was not separate from the poetry. It was the poetry.

text: The Black Death arrived in Sicily in October 1347 aboard Genoese trading ships, and the Sicilians, seeing the sailors covered in black swellings that oozed blood and pus, drove the ships back out of the harbor. It made no difference. Within five years, somewhere between a third and half of Europe's population was dead. What is difficult to hold in mind is the speed. In England, the plague arrived in the summer of 1348 and by spring of 1349 had passed through the country. Villages did not slowly depopulate; they were emptied in weeks. The mechanisms of medieval society, built entirely on the assumption of abundant labor, were simply insufficient to process grief on this scale. Parish churches could not hold enough funerals. Cemeteries ran out of room. Survivors encountered a world in which the material evidence of the dead, their houses, their fields, their unfinished work, was everywhere, while the people themselves had vanished. The long-term consequences were profound and often unexpected: labor shortages gave the surviving peasantry negotiating power they had never possessed, accelerating the collapse of feudal arrangements. The plague was catastrophe, but it was also, for those who lived, a leveraged beginning.

text: The ancient Athenian practice of ostracism was simultaneously a safety valve and a ritual of democratic self-definition. Once a year, if the assembly voted to hold the procedure, citizens would scratch the name of whichever politician they most wished to exile onto a shard of pottery, an ostrakon. The man who received the most votes, provided at least six thousand votes were cast in total, was banished from Attica for ten years, his property intact, no crime charged. He was not being punished for wrongdoing; he was being removed for being too powerful, or too controversial, or simply too present. The procedure was used only about a dozen times across its century of operation, which suggests it functioned as a threat as much as a practice. The names scratched on surviving ostraka include some of the most illustrious in Athenian history: Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon. The system contained its own irony: Aristides was allegedly ostracized because voters had grown tired of hearing him called the Just. A man approached at the polls by a citizen who couldn't write asked Aristides to scratch a name for him; the citizen said he wanted to ostracize Aristides. Aristides wrote his own name, and said nothing.

text: The ziggurat was not a temple but a mountain. The Mesopotamian civilizations of Sumer, Akkad, and Babylon built their enormous stepped platforms not as places of congregation but as artificial high places where the divine could descend to meet the priestly representatives of the city below. The gods, in Mesopotamian cosmology, did not live in temples; they lived in the sky, the deep water, and the storm. The ziggurat was the point of contact, the staircase of meeting. At its summit was a small chamber, furnished, provisioned with food and a bed, where the god might rest during the descent. It was not a place for ordinary worshippers, who conducted their religious life in courts and chapels at the base. text: Herodotus has been called both the Father of History and the Father of Lies, and both epithets are revealing. text: The great Maya collapse of the ninth century CE was not a collapse but a rearrangement. What ended was a particular configuration of political and monumental culture, one organized around the construction of temples and stelae glorifying divine kings. The people who had built those temples outlasted the ideology that motivated them, adapted to new conditions, and continued. This is the pattern that gets lost when historians reach for the word collapse: what falls is rarely everything, and the people who survive are rarely the story's end.

text: Composting at home is simpler than most people assume, and it transforms kitchen waste into something genuinely useful rather than something you feel guilty about throwing away. text: Zone two cardio has had a remarkable resurgence, and for good reason: it's the kind of exercise that's sustainable for decades. text: The tardigrade is less than a millimeter long and looks, under a microscope, like a small bear that has been inflated slightly past its design specifications. text: Iridium is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust, because when the planet was young and molten, nearly all of it sank toward the iron core. text: Water is one of the stranger molecules in chemistry. By the logic of its molecular weight, it should be a gas at room temperature — its chemical cousins hydrogen sulfide and hydrogen selenide are gases, and they are much heavier. Water is liquid because of hydrogen bonding: each molecule has a small positive charge near its hydrogen atoms and a small negative charge near the oxygen, and these opposite charges attract neighboring molecules, creating a loose but persistent lattice of connections that must be broken for the liquid to become vapor. This same structure accounts for the fact that ice is less dense than liquid water — the crystalline arrangement in ice spaces the molecules farther apart than the disordered arrangement in liquid — which is why ice floats rather than sinking. If ice sank, lakes and oceans would freeze from the bottom up, with no insulating ice layer above. The evolution of aquatic life, and perhaps life itself, depended on this structural quirk of a three-atom molecule that follows no obvious rule.

text: Migratory birds navigate in ways that took researchers decades to untangle, and some pieces remain contested. text: Plate tectonics moves slowly enough that most of its consequences are invisible on a human timescale, but it has been the primary architect of everything we recognize as geography. The Atlantic Ocean is widening by roughly the distance your fingernails grow each year. Africa and South America were once joined — their coastlines fit together not as coincidence but as fact, and the fossils of identical species on both sides of the ocean confirm what the shape already suggests. Mountain ranges rise where plates collide, their height the result of how fast they are pushed up versus how fast erosion wears them down. The Himalayas are still growing. The forces involved are planetary in scale: the convection of heat from the Earth's interior, churning the mantle over timescales of millions of years, dragging the rigid surface plates along on currents of rock so slow they are measured in centimeters per year. text: Photosynthesis is the fundamental transaction of the living world: carbon dioxide and water, driven by light, converted into sugar and oxygen. The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes inside the chloroplast, where chlorophyll and other pigments absorb photons and use their energy to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a byproduct and generating the energy currency that powers the next stage. It is not especially efficient — it sometimes grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, running an essentially wasteful side reaction — but no other enzyme has been found to do its job at all, so evolution has compensated by producing enormous quantities of it. text: The deep ocean is the largest habitat on Earth, and one of the least explored. Below about two hundred meters, sunlight fades to nothing, pressure climbs to crushing levels, and temperatures hover just above freezing across most of the seafloor. text: Every element heavier than iron was forged in violence. Iron sits at the peak of nuclear binding energy, which means that fusing iron atoms together costs energy rather than releasing it, and stars cannot sustain fusion past iron. Elements like gold, uranium, and platinum require conditions that can only be achieved in the cores of collapsing massive stars or, more likely, in the mergers of neutron stars — events that last fractions of a second and release more energy than the Sun will emit over its entire lifetime. In 2017, gravitational wave detectors recorded the merger of two neutron stars in a galaxy 130 million light-years away, and telescopes trained on the same location detected a kilonova — the explosion that produced, among other things, gold and platinum in quantities exceeding the mass of Jupiter. The gold in any ring or coin on Earth was made in an event like that, scattered through space by the explosion, eventually gathered into the dust cloud that formed our solar system, and concentrated by geological processes over billions of years before it was found in a riverbed or a vein of rock and fashioned into something meant to last.

text: The spleen is an organ most people know almost nothing about until they are told it might need to be removed. It sits in the upper left abdomen, tucked behind the stomach, and it performs two broad functions: filtering blood and supporting immunity. As a filter, it identifies and removes old or damaged red blood cells, recycling their iron and hemoglobin. As an immune organ, it houses large populations of lymphocytes and macrophages, and it acts as a reservoir for monocytes — white cells that are rapidly deployed to sites of injury or infection. The spleen also holds a reserve of platelets and, under certain conditions, can function as a site of blood cell production. You can live without it, but not entirely without consequence: people who have had their spleen removed face a lifelong elevated risk of serious infections from encapsulated bacteria, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae, and are typically vaccinated and sometimes prescribed prophylactic antibiotics as a result. The organ is soft and highly vascular, which makes it vulnerable to rupture in abdominal trauma — and its rupture is one of the few internal injuries that can cause rapid, life-threatening blood loss.

text: A glacier moves because ice, under sufficient pressure and thickness, deforms and flows. When glaciers melt back, they leave a record in the landscape: the boulders carried from distant quarries and dropped in places where no river could have brought them, called erratics; the ridges of debris pushed up at the glacier's terminus, called moraines. text: The aurora borealis — and its southern counterpart, the aurora australis — is the visible output of a continuous interaction between the Sun and Earth's magnetic field. The Sun constantly emits a stream of charged particles called the solar wind, which strikes Earth's magnetosphere and deforms it: compressed on the sunward side, stretched into a long tail on the night side. text: Soil is not simply ground-up rock, though rock particles form the mineral component. A tablespoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms than there are humans on Earth — bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes, and archaea engaged in a community of processes that determine whether anything can grow. text: When Voyager 1 crossed a boundary roughly eleven billion miles from the Sun in 2012, it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. text: Cephalopods — octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish — are colorblind by the standard measure: they have only a single type of photoreceptor, where color vision in humans depends on three. text: Most software projects fail not because of bad code but because of bad abstractions. An abstraction is a bet: you are betting that the boundary you draw today will still make sense when the system grows. A leaky abstraction forces every layer above it to know about the details below, which means the boundary never held in the first place. The reason experienced engineers spend so much time arguing about interfaces and module boundaries is that those decisions compound in both directions. Good abstractions stay invisible — they simply do what you expect and nothing else. Bad ones become the subject of tribal knowledge, the thing you learn about only when you break it. text: Attention is the scarce resource that the entire consumer internet was built to capture, and the business models that emerged from that scarcity have shaped behavior at a civilizational scale. text: Retrieval-augmented generation, the technique of giving a language model access to a searchable knowledge base at inference time, solves a real problem but introduces a subtler one. The real problem is that model weights are a lossy, static encoding of information from a fixed point in time. Plugging in retrieval means the system can cite recent facts and cite them accurately. The subtler problem is that retrieval quality is now the ceiling of answer quality, and retrieval quality is genuinely hard to evaluate. A model that confidently synthesizes two slightly wrong retrieved passages will produce a confident, plausible-sounding, wrong answer. This failure mode is harder to catch than hallucination from parametric memory, because the system will often produce a citation alongside the error. The practical implication is that RAG systems need at least as much investment in their retrieval pipeline — chunking strategy, embedding quality, reranking — as in the generation layer that most developers find more interesting.

text: The spaced repetition algorithm is one of the most robustly validated findings in cognitive science and one of the least used tools in mainstream education. The core insight, which dates to Ebbinghaus in the 1880s, is that memory traces decay in a predictable curve, and that reviewing material just as it is about to be forgotten dramatically extends long-term retention at a fraction of the total study time. text: Open source software is one of the stranger economic phenomena of the modern era. text: The most important thing about a pricing strategy is that it is a positioning statement disguised as a number. text: Serverless computing promised to eliminate the operational overhead of managing infrastructure, and it largely delivered on that promise for specific workloads. Functions that run briefly, respond to events, and scale to zero when idle are genuinely well-served by the model. text: The productivity literature has a consistent structural problem: it is written predominantly by people whose jobs involve producing text, and it treats text production as the paradigmatic form of knowledge work. text: Type systems in programming languages are a form of machine-checked documentation that travels with the code and degrades gracefully with refactoring. When you change the shape of a data structure in a strongly-typed codebase, the compiler tells you everywhere that assumption was made. text: The network effect is invoked so broadly in technology strategy that it has lost most of its analytical precision. In its narrow and genuine form, a network effect means that each additional user makes the product more valuable to all existing users — not just marginally, not hypothetically, but in a way a user can concretely experience. These are real advantages, but they are different from true network effects because they saturate, because they do not prevent fragmentation, and because they cannot by themselves explain why a platform should dominate a category indefinitely. Using the term loosely leads strategists to build for defensibility they do not actually have.

text: Marginal cost pricing for digital goods produces a structural contradiction that most content businesses are still working around. text: Observability in software systems is the property that allows you to understand what a system is doing from its outputs, without needing to know in advance what questions you will ask. text: Prediction markets work better than expert panels at forecasting geopolitical and economic events, and this finding has been robust enough across enough experiments that it should have changed institutional practice more than it has.
